claims.claim: Project initiation can be understood as defining a proposed project or phase sufficiently to obtain authorization to start it.
A sponsor is generally connected to the project’s perceived need and has a role in authorizing its start; the exact role and authority vary by setting.

GAO’s IT investment framework states that business needs for each IT project should be identified and defined, and names business purpose during initiation and an executive sponsor as ways to establish the link to a need or mission goal.
The same GAO framework identifies specific users for each IT project and describes user participation through the project life cycle.

PMI’s sponsorship and stakeholder-alignment discussion says early stakeholder identification helps reveal organizations and individuals who need involvement and the support or contributions that may be needed.

The lesson’s treatment of unanswered questions as a reason for further investigation, a limited next step, or a pause is an educational inference from initiation’s decision purpose, not a universal organizational procedure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources describe initiation within differing organizational contexts.
positions: PMI discusses sponsorship and stakeholder alignment in a general professional context.
GAO provides a public-sector IT investment-management framework with specific business-need and user practices.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses only their shared high-level ideas of purpose, authorization, sponsor, and early stakeholder identification. It labels the GAO material as a bounded illustration and does not prescribe either source’s process.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft offered generic initiation language without source-backed distinctions between authorization, sponsorship, high-level goals, and stakeholder identification.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic boilerplate with a source-verified account of initiation as a decision-and-alignment stage.
Excluded charter, scope, requirements, and detailed planning content owned by sibling topics.
Added original hypothetical examples that identify uncertainty without offering organizational advice.
rightsIssues: PMI material was read live and treated as REFERENCE_ONLY; no PMI prose, diagrams, or templates were reproduced.
GAO’s framework is a U.S. government publication. The lesson uses original prose and reproduces no source text, tables, or diagrams.

questionKeyCheck.method: Read every saved prompt, all four options, correctIndex, explanation, and sourceIds after writing.
questionKeyCheck.result: Exactly five four-option questions; every key is supported and unambiguous; keys span A through D with no position used more than twice; the bank includes recall, application, and analysis.

sourceRecords.title: How do we start a project? Ensuring the right sponsorship, stakeholder alignment and thoughtful preparation for a project
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. Supports the role of early project purpose, sponsorship, initial information gaps, and stakeholder identification. It is an authored PMI learning-library article rather than a universal rule; original prose only and no templates or wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Information Technology Investment Management: A Framework for Assessing and Improving Process Maturity, Version 1
sourceRecords.notes: Read live, especially pages 53–58. Supports the bounded IT example: define business needs, identify users, link a project to a need or mission goal, identify an executive sponsor, and support user participation. The lesson does not treat this 2000 federal IT framework as a universal project-initiation process.
